en.title: Shopping
en.goal: Ask prices (with numbers up to one hundred), try on clothes and buy in a store.

phrases.scenario: You're in a store and want to know the price of a product. What do you ask?
A customer asks the price of a product that costs forty euros. What do you answer?

phrases.t: Can I try on these pants?
phrases.scenario: You're in a clothing store and want to try on pants before buying. What do you ask?
You're the salesperson and need to charge the customer one hundred euros. What do you say?

dialogue.title: In a store
lines: Hello, I'm looking for a dress.
I'm a 38. How much is it?

voudrais-vs-peux.title: "Je voudrais" or "je peux"?
voudrais-vs-peux.body: Je voudrais (I would like) is the politest way to ask for something in a store — it sounds kinder than "je veux" (I want). Je peux...? (Can I...?) is used to ask permission, like trying on clothes: je peux essayer ce pantalon? Both are polite, but they serve different moments: asking for something vs. asking permission.

combien-ca-coute-wh-in-situ.title: "Combien ça coûte ?" also becomes "Ça coûte combien ?"
combien-ca-coute-wh-in-situ.body: Notice that the dialogue you just read already uses the everyday form: Ça coûte combien ? instead of "Combien ça coûte ?". In everyday speech, it's common to move the question word to the end of the sentence. In the exercises here, keep using "Combien ça coûte ?" — it's the form the exercises ask for.

review.why: FR 'pas cher' is neutral ('not expensive'); EN 'cheap' can sound negative, so I added 'inexpensive'
EN-US 'pants' (EN-GB 'trousers'); FR 'pantalon' is singular but EN is plural

review.pt: A loja fecha às dezenove horas.
review.why: FR uses 24h 'dix-neuf heures'; converted to 7 p.m. for natural EN-US
FR 'Quelle taille faites-vous ?' is formal (vous); EN 'What size do you wear?' also works
'Je fais du 38' = 'I wear a 38'; European sizing
'May I...?' is more formal and also correct
